language.script_notes: English and French are both official nationwide (bilingual federal signage); French is dominant in Quebec specifically, English dominant elsewhere. Speed limits are posted in km/h — a reliable way to rule out the US at a glance.

road_furniture.bollard_color: Varies distinctly by province — see regional profiles for Quebec's thin white guardrail-mounted bollards, Ontario's diamond markers, and the Northwest Territories' black-and-white striped cylindrical bollards.
road_furniture.guardrail_type: Standard steel W-beam nationally, with provincial variations in attached reflectors/markers.
road_furniture.line_paint: White outside/yellow inside lines nationally — distinct from the more US-typical all-yellow-center convention.
road_furniture.curb_style: Well-maintained painted kerbs in cities nationwide.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Esso, Irving, Petro-Canada, Husky Energy and Ultramar are common fuel-station brands. Ontario's speed-limit signs explicitly include a 'km/h' label at the bottom in white text on black.

architecture.roof_style: Steep-pitched roofs nationwide given snow load; the classic 'Ontario Style House' (rectangular wood-frame with a gable over the short side and a smaller entrance gable) is a recognizable historic Ontario form.
architecture.roof_material: Asphalt shingle widespread; metal roofing common in snowier/rural areas.
architecture.wall_construction: Wood-frame siding construction is the national default, similar to the US; French Catholic church architecture in Quebec did not adopt the High Gothic Revival style common in Ontario/Maritime churches — a subtle regional architectural difference.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Muted, weather-resistant tones nationwide; regional variation covered in profiles.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Wood-frame single-family houses nationwide; grain elevators across the Prairies; Quebec's distinctive church architecture; lighthouses along the Maritime coast.

nature.vegetation: Extremely varied given the country's enormous size — dense mixed/boreal forest across most of the country, flat prairie farmland in the west-central provinces, temperate rainforest on the Pacific coast, and Arctic tundra in the far north. See regional profiles.
nature.terrain: The world's second-largest country by area — the Canadian Shield's forest and lakes cover much of the center-east, the Rocky Mountains and Coast Mountains dominate the west, flat prairie fills the west-central provinces, and Arctic terrain covers the far north.
nature.climate_signature: Cold winters nationwide with heavy snow common in Street View imagery; strong regional variation from temperate coastal rainforest to Arctic tundra.

vehicles.plate_color: Varies distinctly by province — Ontario white with blue text ('Yours to Discover'), Quebec blue-on-white with a fleur-de-lis, Alberta red-on-white ('Wild Rose Country'), British Columbia blue-on-white with a screened provincial flag, and the Northwest Territories' famous polar-bear-shaped plate.
vehicles.plate_format: Varies by province; commonly a letter/digit mix.
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: Pickup trucks and SUVs are disproportionately common as in the US; provincial plate design/colour is one of the single best in-country location clues.

google_coverage.camera_generation: Mix of Gen 3/4 in populated areas; Gen 1/2 in some older rural coverage.
google_coverage.coverage_notes: Dense across the populated south; genuine coverage exists in the far north but is extremely sparse — limited to a handful of highways and towns (see North Canada profile).

confusion_set.shared_traits: English signage nationwide outside Quebec, similar wood-frame suburban architecture, similar pickup-truck culture near the shared border
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Canadian speed-limit signs are posted in km/h (vs. US mph); Canadian plates carry a province name (not a US state), and Canada has universal bilingual federal signage (English/French) that the US lacks.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared French language and some similar Catholic church architecture in Quebec specifically
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Quebec's road furniture (bollards, plate format, km/h signage) is distinctly North American/Canadian, not French; the surrounding wood-frame architecture and grid-pattern suburban development look nothing like rural France.
